slides.title:
All Cultures,
All Races
slides.hook:
Here’s how we handle your wedding culture
and traditions with care and precision.

slides.quote: We met 4 planners, 2 of Indian origin and 2 of Indonesian. We finally shortlisted BaliVIP, despite the Indian origin wedding planners having more experience in Indian weddings and knowing the customs better, because in our conversations with Veronika and Casavia we found a willingness to be flexible and customize the wedding to the way our children had imagined it.

slides.lead:
An Indian wedding needs
four or five separate spaces.
slides.body:
Across two or three days.
Count your events, not your guests.

Ceremony, then reception. Two spaces, one evening,
and every hour of it built to feel intimate.

slides.lead:
A Chinese wedding can run sangjit,
ceremony, tea pai and reception.
slides.body:
A tea ceremony needs a real indoor room,
close to the action. A lawn is not a room.

slides.lead:
A baraat needs a driveway
and room to turn around.
slides.body:
Some of Bali’s best venues are reached
single file down a cliff path. Ask how the groom arrives.

slides.lead:
A tea ceremony is quiet
and close. A sangeet
is loud and late.
slides.body:
Same lighting, same playlist and same pacing
for both, and each one feels slightly wrong.

From Jain to halal, vegetarian, no beef and allergies.
We ask whether the kitchen can run a separate prep line.

slides.lead:
Some traditions center
on the couple. Others bring
in parents and family.
slides.body:
Vows can belong to the two of you alone.
Other rituals need your parents present.
We ask which is which before the run sheet is printed.

slides.lead:
We work with you and your
parents, not around them.
slides.body:
Every tradition, every responsibility,
every family expectation. We ask who has to be
present for what, and build the timeline around it.

Haldi, sangjit, tea pai, akad, baraat, whatever
your family runs. We come back the same day with
how many spaces you need and which venues fit.
